ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, a conducting circular ring with radius L is located in the plane of the paper, and O is the center of the circle. Uniform magnetic fields are distributed in two sector-shaped regions inside the ring whose central angles are 90° and which are centrally symmetric about O; the magnitudes of the magnetic induction intensities of the two magnetic fields are both B, their directions are opposite, and both are perpendicular to the plane of the paper. The conducting rod OM can rotate about O, and the M end is in good contact with the circular ring through a sliding contact. A resistor R is connected between the center of the circle and the circular ring. The resistance of the circular ring and the conducting rod is neglected. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the conducting circular ring is in the plane of the paper, the center of the circle is labeled O, and there is a conducting rod OM in the radial direction, with the M end in contact with the circular ring; in the external circuit on the right there is a resistor R and an ideal ammeter A. Inside the circular ring there are two 90° sector-shaped magnetic field regions centrally symmetric about O: the upper-right sector uses “×” to indicate that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the paper and inward, and the lower-left sector uses “·” to indicate that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the paper and outward; the remaining two 90° sector-shaped regions have no magnetic field. The arrow in the figure indicates that rod OM rotates counterclockwise with angular velocity ω. Reasoning: When the entire conducting rod is located within a certain uniform magnetic field 90° sector, the velocity of a small segment of the rod at distance r from O is v=ωr, and the generated motional electromotive force element is dε=Bωrdr. Integrating along the rod from 0 to L gives the magnitude of the electromotive force ε0=∫0^L Bωrdr=BL^2ω/2. Therefore the corresponding current magnitude is I0=ε0/R=BL^2ω/(2R). According to the regions passed through in one revolution in the figure, when the rod is in the upper-right 90° sector, the current is +I0, lasting one quarter of a period; then in the no-field 90° region the current is 0, lasting one quarter of a period; when it is in the lower-left 90° sector, the magnetic field direction is opposite, the electromotive force direction is opposite, and the current is -I0, lasting one quarter of a period; finally in the other no-field 90° region the current is 0, lasting one quarter of a period. The reading of the ideal ammeter takes the effective value, so Irms=sqrt[(I0^2·1/4)+0+(I0^2·1/4)+0]=I0/√2=√2BL^2ω/(4R).
